blocks.x: That's the first thing I'm going to do. They can take your trumpet mouthpiece and duplicate it then for the coronet. Yes. You see... Or you can get a bigger shank, you know, a little tube to put around it too that will fit in it. Yours is big, it has to be smaller for the coronet. Yeah. So you can't do that.
No, I don't think it...
No, there's nothing you can do.
I think it would interfere with the sound of the coronet if you did that.
Yeah, it would make it too long and tune everything out of it.

But I, naturally, I've been in and out of New York since 1939 and last time I was there, I had a coronet mouthpiece made, but as good as the mouthpieces this man makes, he doesn't have a...I don't know what you call it now, what would you call it? A mold. In other words, if he makes you a mouthpiece, he doesn't have a duplicate mold if you wanted another one.
Yeah. In other words, he... They usually put them on a lathe. I've seen Rudy Muck make them. That is the thing I'm talking about.

He doesn't have...he...when he makes you a mouthpiece, he doesn't take the lathe and...and have a duplicate. Yeah. So when you go there... You have to hold it and look at it. Right. When you go there, he's not going to make the mouthpiece exactly. No. See? Because if he had that mold, then he could just go by that mold.

Well, you said something about being in New York, the first...like since 1939. I remember that's the first New Orleans band I really heard in person. That was 1936 when you were up at Nick's. Remember down there? You go down a few steps to the old Nick's on 7th Avenue.

That's right. It was in 1939. It was...when I went to New York, it was 1936. When I went to work for Nick, it was going into 1937. Yeah. In other words, this is how I got to New York. I just finished a place called the Chapery. It's right out here in West End. It's now the Maison Restaurant. Oh yeah. This was the Chapery. It was run by Joe Loicana, Steve Loicana, and Angelo Gemelli. They had a nightclub. And it was a pretty big place. Yeah. And at that time, they had a woman by the name of Ming Toy. She was a striptease. In other words, she didn't dance or take her clothes off. She used to dance like Sally Rand with the fans. Oh yeah. And it'd become a big hit here. So I played there for about a year or so, and left there, and I wasn't doing anything at all. And I don't know if you know this man, his name is Ray Bonitas, he plays a wonderful bass. But I know you know Frank Frederica. Oh yes. Oh yeah. So Wingy Menor is in New York, and he sends for Frank Frederica and Ray Bonitas to come up to New York. He had a job waiting for them. And Ray Bonitas and Frank are very good friends of mine. So they said, come take a ride to New York with us. And I said, well what am I going to do in New York? I don't have no job. You fellas have a job. They said, come on. This Ray Bonitas, he's always had a lot of money. His people had a lot of money. So they said, don't worry about anything. Just come on. If you feel like you want to go back home, I'll just give you the money and you can go back home. So we got to New York, and we were there about a week. And Ben Pollack came to New York. Now you know Ben Pollack. And they had a fine band. And in other words he had Farzola.
Is Harry James one of those names?
Harry James. He had the trombone player. He was in the Army and got lost in the plane. Glenn Miller he had. Ray Badu. Eddie Miller. Snappy Lamar. He had all of them.
Oh yeah, that old band he had with Benny Goodman and other.
Right.
Benny was in the band a little earlier before that I guess.
And he said, I'm glad you're in town. We're going to make some records with the big band and if you want to make a session, I'll be glad to arrange it for you.
What did I have to lose?
I said, well I'll be more than happy to. So he got me a date and it was with Brunswick. That's right, Brunswick. They made another label called Vocalion.
Yeah, I remember those black label vocalions, gold printing on them.

So we got Farz, Ben Pollack was on the drums, Santo Pecora played the trombone, and Eddie Miller played the sax. Eddie Condon played the guitar. And a fellow by the name of Al Hort was a piano player, a Negro, but he was a fine piano player. So to make a long story short, we made a session, and we made a good session at that time, and I got a contract.
Yeah, I remember those records.

So I got a contract to record for Brunswick, which held me over in New York. I didn't have nothing to worry about then, and then I got paid, you know, and I got a little royalty. So I stayed in New York, and Nick Rangetti, the place that I played in the village, he knew about me. He didn't know me, but he knew about me through a fellow by the name of Sidney Harriton. Oh yeah. You remember him? I never knew him. He had died before I got there.
Wonderful client. Wonderful, yeah.

And he used to talk to Nick a lot about me, see. So Nick found out that I was in New York, and he sent for me, and I went down and talked to him, and he said, I'd like to have you put a band in my place. So I said, I'd be happy to. He says, they never did have jazz here. All we had was piano players and singers, but I think that maybe we put a jazz band in here.
It might create something. It's a little tiny place. I hardly remember.
It was in the cellar.
Yeah, I remember.

In other words, it was a cobweb place. Yeah, I heard you there. Down in the cellar. And so I got a band together, George Brunus. George Brunus. First time I heard George in person. Bill Bourgeois, a fella by the name of Turk on the bass, and Bowman. I don't know if you know Bowman, Red Bowman, he played piano.
Yeah, yeah, the pianist. He was from New York, I guess.

Yes, and Johnny Castang. Yeah. And they didn't expect any big things to happen, but it just clicked, Bill. From then on he went into the band business. From then on, in fact, we made him enough money to build the new Knicks.
That place across the street, yeah.
And we played there for about a year or something. That's where he made all his money and he built a new place called Knicks.

In those days I was traveling around the country a lot. I was in the Depression and every time I'd come back to town, my friend would say, Steve Smith, say, you should have been here last week. Larry Shields sat in with the band. Yeah, yes. I never did get to hear Larry. Never in my life. He never? Only on record.
Oh, he played wonderful, wonderful. Well, in fact, Tommy Dorsey, Jimmy Dorsey, all of them came down and they'd sit in. We'd had a ball in that place.

I'm sorry, most of all I missed Shields, the only chance I ever had to hear him. Then they got that Dixieland band together and traveled around the country and I just missed them in Memphis and I missed them down here about 1937. Yeah, I played with them. Yeah, you made some records then when La Rocca left.
La Rocca left and came back home and I was finished at Nix and they asked me would I join them and I joined them. Did you travel with them?
Oh, yeah.

We went to... Oh, I wasn't sure if you traveled with them. Yes, we went to Oklahoma, Houston, Texas, Shreveport. Well, I forgot that you traveled, yeah, on that tour. I traveled with them for quite a while and I hate... there's another thing that I don't like to say, but they couldn't get along.
Yeah, well, I mean La Rocca has told that story too, he always complained. Yeah, but... Everybody blamed everybody else, so... That's right.

You see, when we'd get on a bandstand and when it come time to play a number, well, one would say, let's play this and everyone would say, oh, let's play this, let's play that. And we'd be organ five, ten minutes before we'd get to play one tune. So I'd say, oh, let's play this and I'd just go off with it. Yeah, that's the way you do. So I got tired of that. I said, I'm going home.
Yeah. Well, Eddie Edwards is dead now too, I guess. He was the manager, I guess, in a way, and tried to run it, and then La Rocca was the leader, or so it was a...
Well, it was a co-op thing, and everybody had the same say-so, and that is where the trouble was.
The trumpet ought to be the leader, though, in a New Orleans band. That's right. It's a tradition to have the leader. Right.

They should have a man to do all the business, and after he'd do that business, then all get together and say, now, this is what's going to happen. We'll play here so and so, so and so. See? After all, they organized that band to make money, which they did make a lot of money, but
they should have made more. Yeah, yeah. Well, another trip of yours I just thought of last night was going to ask you about that Hadacall trip. I guess they still owe you money for that, do they?

Yeah. Now, that was a fabulous thing, Bill. Yeah, I never... The first, the first show, there were two shows. Yeah. Now, the first show, they traveled in bus, big bus, Greyhound bus. They'd take all the performers and the entertainer and the musician.
When was that? I forget, was that in the 40s?
No, no, it was 1951. That late?
That late, I forgot.
And then they had another one in 1952.
Oh, that late.
Now, that was the one where they went bankrupt. Yeah. And he sold the Hadacall company to some other medical...
Do they still make the stuff? I don't remember seeing it ever. Yes, they make it. It's on the market. It's still on the market. I wasn't sure. Yeah.

In other words, he over-promoted himself. Yeah, he must have. Now, he could have made a lot of money, but in other words, he would hire... The last show they had, he had a 16-coach train. Oh, yeah. That's good. Now, that's a lot of money.
Too beautiful.
And everybody on the show could go in the diner and eat and just sign a tale. Yeah. It was marvelous for the entertainers and the help, but he could... It was too expensive.
Yeah, finally got too much. Yeah.

So, we finally got to Dallas and that was the end. And not only did he owe me money, he owes everybody... I guess everybody. ...that was on the show. Jimmy Durante, Milton Boyle, and... They were all on that show. Count Carmen Miranda, Dick Haynes. He owes them all money. Yeah, he had the biggest things. The electricians, the sound equipment, the carpenters, they all got it.
And that was the end of the Hattie call. It was a good idea while it lasted. Oh, he had a money.

Yeah. Well, do you know how many people we used to play there at one time? No. $50,000. Really? Yes. Where'd they do it? The admission to the shows, you had to have a box top of Hattie call. Yeah. Now, I think the Hattie call sold for a dollar and a half up to $3. So, either one, if you had a dollar and a half box or a $3 box, that was your admission. Yeah. And 40 and 50 thousand people. Now, you figure that out.
Yeah.
That was a lot of money.
Yeah, it was good profit in that medicine. Right.
But his expenses was too great. Yeah.
Yeah.

Where did you play? In the outdoors and stadiums? Well, you see, to accommodate people like that, 40, 50 thousand people, we played in football stadiums, in baseball parks, in all big places like that. Because you could never get that many people in a theater or an auditorium.
Oh, no, no.
At that time, they didn't have auditoriums that big. No. No.

Let's see if there's anything about the, we kept talking about those later things, anything about in the early days, which we're trying to get all that early history, which most people have forgotten. Can you remember, you said you worked with Brownlee for a while and made those first records, I guess that was your first record date? That was the first record. That was down here, wasn't it? Right here, yeah.

An okay record made. Yeah, it was on Barone Street in Greenwalls. Had you been working with Brownlee for a while, or? Yes, Brownlee was the only band that I wasn't the leader of. After that, I started off as a leader, and then I went to work with Brownlee for a while, and then I organized my band again, and I've been a leader ever since.
He's still over in Pensacola, I think, still. Yes, I think so. Connected to the union over there, I believe they say.
Yes, I think so. I haven't seen him in quite a while, but the last time I've seen him, he looked wonderful. I've never met him. Oh, he was a wonderful fellow.

A friend of ours, Paul Crawford, remember the trombonist, he works for Tulane University too, and he interviewed Brownlee over there at Pensacola. He did? Yeah. About four or five years ago. I guess he's still living and working there.
He was a very good salesman, a very good promoter. How was he? A pretty good pianist. Wonderful piano player.
Wonderful.

I forgot to hear him. He could make a banjo talk. But it wasn't his instrument. The piano was his instrument. But he was a salesman of instruments, so he played the banjo, the ukulele, to sell the instruments.
I believe Tom Brown was on that record. Did he play with you all regularly in that band?
No. No. Tom Brown didn't play with us regularly.
Joe Lloyd Canner. Do you remember who else was in the band? Yeah. I may have made a note of some of the people who were on the record, but I was wondering about where did you work with the band?

Well it was what they call a spot job band. In other words they'd play, maybe tonight they'd play Over the River, and the next night they'd play here, West Wego, all around us. What they call a spot job band here. Yeah.
Casual engagements. Harry Shields was on that record. Harry Shields played.

Did he play with you much in those days? Yes. Yes. Mostly. Harry mostly played the clarinet with me all the time. There was Harry Shields, Brown Lee, Joe Lloyd Canner, myself, and I can't think of his name, but it was Brown Lee's brother-in-law that played the banjo.
Oh I have a note on the record, it was French, Barrowman French. That's his name, yeah.
And Crum, Crum, Crum, Crum, Crum, Crum, Crum, Crum, Crum, I think it was something like that. I just can't remember.

Yeah, a drummer, Alonzo Crumby. Alonzo Crumby, right. I was going to ask about Harry Shields. I never got to hear his brother, older brother. Do you think their styles are a good deal the same? I like Harry's playing very much and it sounds to me somewhat... The sounds are practically the same.

The only difference was that Larry got a bigger tone. Bigger tone, yeah. Now Harry gets a wonderful tone. But Larry got a bigger tone, deeper. And the styles were practically the same. But he did have a bigger tone, yeah. Oh yeah. In fact, Larry Shields has the biggest tone I've ever heard on the clarinet.
Really? Yeah. Yeah, I didn't know that. Nobody ever told... You can't tell from the record, you see, but I didn't know that.
Oh, when he played in the middle register, in the low register, it sounded like a bassoon.
Yeah.
And clear as a bell.

Yeah. Because Harry gets an awfully good tone, especially up high. He gets a good, loud, clear tone that other people can't do anymore, it looks like. Right in tune and all three. Larry got a bigger tone than that.
Bigger tone, yeah.
That's remarkable. Yeah, I wish I could have heard him.
Well, I can say this much for Larry. He, in other words, inspired a lot of clarinet players. In fact, all of them. Yeah. Because he was the first man on records.

The St. Louis Blues Chorus, you know the one I mean where he starts on a high note and holds a... Harry plays it. Yeah, Harry plays it like... Exactly like that. But Larry got a bigger tone. Yeah. Did Larry make up that chorus? Do you think that's the first one you ever heard play that? Yeah, oh yeah. Yeah, Larry made that chorus up.
In other words, he could slow a clarinet better than anybody that I've known.

I wish I'd heard him. Yeah. Too late now. Any other favorite clarinet players you can think of that you've played with that you... Well, I mentioned Sidney Ayrton. Yeah, Sidney Ayrton. I never got to hear him.
Charlie Cadella.
Yeah.
Leon Rapolo.
He's still around I guess.
I don't know. Charlie's still here and every now and then he plays. He will?
Yeah. Plays mostly sax or does he play clarinet and sax?
No, no he plays clarinet and sax but he... I don't know, he just lost all interest in it.
Did you ever play with rap Rapolo?
Yes. We played at a nightclub. That was before that time too.
They called them cabarets at that time.
It was on Ramport and Carni. Coochie's plays he used to call it.
You see that place. Yeah. You see Tom Anderson had one place up there. Well no that's...
That was up near Canal. Yeah, but that's a little before my time. Yeah.
I don't remember.
Armstrong played in there. Yeah, he talks about that place.
Where the Tencent store is now I think.
Yeah, that's right. The other place you played at Conti and... And Ramport. Ramport.
Yeah. Coochie's. Coochie's. Coochie's. Coochie's. Coochie's Nightclub. Coochie's.
Yeah. And Ramp, myself, and Joe Guiro played the piano, and Leo Addy played drums, and Joe Loikana played the bass. It was a small combo. No trombone. Yeah.
No trombone. How did rap sound? Does the record sound a very beautiful tone?

Now there's another man that used to get a marvelous tone. Did he have a big tone too? Big, big, round tone. Big, big, round tone. You see when he recorded, they didn't have the equipment to bring out the...
No, he didn't. But even there you can tell beautiful quality, beautiful tone. Right. Like the Tin Roof Blues he made. That's right.

They didn't have the equipment to bring out that tone. No. No. When the boys made a record, the bass and the bass drum, you couldn't use them. Because if you happened to hit on the bass drum it knocked the needle right out of the wax. The same with the bass. If you pull it like that, slap it, it knocked the needle right out of the wax. So therefore we had to play just with wood blocks on the rim of the little drum. And that was a handicap because you were used to hearing rhythm.
Oh yeah, sure.
But today no. Every instrument, in fact every instrument has its own mic. Drum, piano, bass, they all have their own mic.
Yeah. I was going to ask you, I just happen to think, keep changing the subject about you're left handed I guess.
Well I'm naturally left handed Bill. And naturally when I picked up the cornet I had a tendency to play it left handed. Yeah. And I... Did it bother you any? No real handicap then?
No.
In other words, a left handed person has the same amount of ability with his left hand as
a right hand man has. Of course the horn is made sort of to hold easier the other way around the valve. Yeah. It doesn't bother you.
No, no. Naturally I have to put my hand over the bell of the instrument. Yeah.
But it doesn't bother me.
No, because I don't hold the horn straight. I slant the horn.
You're used to it now anyway.
Yeah. Oh, no trouble at all.

Not very many people played the bass or those, I noticed when you were showing how Chink or different people would play the bass you'd do it left handed too. I guess Sherwood's the only left handed bass player I know.
Yeah. Sherwood and, wait they have another one. Is there another one there? I think there's another fella plays with Doth Angels.
I don't know his name but he plays left handed too. Maybe I've seen him in and forgot about it.
Yeah, he played left handed. Yeah.
It's a little more trouble for them. They have to change the stringing of the bass and the round, change the bridge and sound post and all that. Well I don't think it's much trouble, no.

No. And the guitar players all they've got to do is change the strings. Yeah, change the strings and it's all ready to go. Because you have the same technique in, well if I was to play guitar I'd have the same technique that you have in your left hand I'd have it in my right hand.

Yeah, that's right. Yeah. Well I was going to ask about the one, one of your earliest records is the one called Monk Hazel and his Bienville Roof Orchestra under the leadership or under direction of Sharkey, Bonanno it was called.
Yes, that was a...
Did you play there with Monk on the Bienville Roof for a while?

Yes, I played with Monk on the Bienville Roof. We had, in fact we had two trumpets on the roof but we only had one trumpet when we made the record. Yeah. The other trumpet player, his name was Charlie Wagner.
Oh I've heard of him, he was out in Metry, he died just a year or two ago.
That was when we were playing on the Bienville Roof. Now when we made the record... It was down by Lee Circle? Yes, that's an office building now.
Yeah, it's an office building, I never knew from how it was a hotel.
That was a nice hotel. Yeah. They had a nice roof up there. Yeah. Roof up there, yeah.
I never got the seat up. Yeah.
And Monk had a fine band. They had a real good band. In fact we made some real good records there at that time.
Yeah, in high society. That was a wonderful session. That was a wonderful session. Sizzling, yes, and that's a very good record. And did you work there long with him or...?
Yes, we worked there a whole season. Whole season. Mm-hmm. Well in fact it was one of the outstanding places at that time.

Yeah, it must have been. See, like the Blue Room is today, well that was the Bienville Roof. I remember I heard you at the Blue Room in 1938 when I, one of the first times I came to town. Here, after I heard you in New York. You were back, where didn't the Blue Room? Yeah, no, the Fontaine Lounge. Oh yeah, maybe that's where it was, yeah. At least the Rocheville Hotel. Yeah, that's right. The Fontaine Lounge, yeah. I was going to ask about another early record you made back in the 20's with Johnny Miller. And Sidney Aroden is on there. That's right. Plays the Bindler. Yeah. Dipper Mouth and Panama. Dipper Mouth, Panama. I think you made some other tunes. They only brought out the one record I believe though. Is that right? I think so, just those two sides. I believe, Panama and Dipper Mouth.
Yeah, well I heard Panama and the Dipper Mouth.
That's right. Have you worked with Johnny Miller? I never did know much about him.
Well Johnny Miller, he was an engineer on the ships.
Oh, is that right?

Oh, very good engineer, yeah. And every now and then he'd make a trip on the ships and then he'd come back and he'd play piano for a while. Until he felt like he wanted to make another trip, then he'd go and make another trip. But he was a very good piano player.
Yeah. Very good.
He had the records. Very good. And he got the session. So we all made the records. Sidney Airdin, Joe Larcanna, I think it was Monk Hazel, Chink Martin.
Yeah.
Practically the same group. Yeah.
So Johnny Miller didn't work regularly then I guess as a musician. I never did get to hear him or meet him.

No he'd do just like I said. He'd play the piano for a while and he'd get the urge to make a trip. He'd just take out his union card and get on a ship. And an engineer on a ship, Bill, they always make good money. See there's, in other words there's three of them. There's first, second, and third engineers on those ships. The big ocean going. Yes, yes. He'd become a lieutenant commander in the Coast Guard during the war because of being an engineer.

That was 1928. Well I was going to ask, there was a, I looked up in a record book just yesterday and they say there's a rumor that you made some early records even with Jimmy Durante and a group that would have had to have been in New York. They were just probably guessing at it. But do you remember, did you ever make any? Yes. In the early 20s. Yes. Did you?

Yes, we made some records with Jimmy Durante. In fact, I worked with Jimmy Durante, oh I think it was about, I'd say about three or four months in a place called the College Inn on 125th Street. Oh really up there?
Yeah. Do you remember when that was?
It was in, I think it was 25. I'm not positive. And they had Sidney Arden. Yeah. And Johnny Stein.
Yeah, I was going to say the drummer was up there. He worked with Jimmy Durante a long time.
And Jimmy Durante.

They say the record, they made it, somebody had a test record for Victor but it was never issued. No it was not. It was written up in an English book there. I just wondered, I'd never heard about it. It was never released. And this is Johnny Stein, he was the record of the drummer I guess, Jimmy for a long time. Quite a while. Do you remember, that was about 1925 you were in New York.
I think it was about 1925.
Well I think once I heard a rumor you played with the Wolverines for a while or something too, was that in New York?
Yes. Well I could never tell anybody this story because I never had the opportunity. Now Vicks went with Weidman and they sent for me to play the trumpet.
Yeah.

So I agreed and I went to New York to play the trumpet with the Wolverine. Now they played a lot of numbers that I practically didn't know. So I said, well why don't we have one or two rehearsals so I can understand the numbers
that you are playing. Yeah, so they were from Chicago over that way where they played different tunes.
And they had a couple of fellas in the band. It was a little temperamental. And they couldn't see to having a little rehearsal. Yeah, afternoon bands, I know what you mean.
You know what I mean? I know what you mean.

So I said, listen fellas, if you don't want to have a rehearsal and we are going to get along like this, it's best that you gave me fair to go back home because I'd rather be home contented than to be playing discontented.
Yeah, that's right.
So that's what happened. I played for a week with them and in fact I demanded my money because that was in the agreement.
That's the best thing to do, yeah.
And they finally gave me the money and I came home and Jimmy Mack Partland went in the band.

Oh yeah, I knew him and Chicago. He's still around New York now. Yeah. And that was the episode of the Wolverines. Yeah, was that about the, that wasn't the same trip then with Jimmy Durante all up there? It was after, after.
It was after that. After Jimmy Durante's trip. Yeah.

Yeah, I wish you could have heard that record that, was Frank Christian, he played up there a long time, was he? He wouldn't be there of course if you were the trumpet. Yes, Frank Christian was. Was he around then too?
No, he, he had the job before me. He had the job, that's what then you, you.

Yes, way before me. Yeah, that's what I wondered. We interviewed him almost two years ago and he told us quite a bit about that band but he didn't talk much about Jimmy Durante. I'd hoped he'd tell us more about him, you know, because he's a funny guy and a great entertainer and all. Jimmy and. And you never did get him to tell them much about that band.

Well Jimmy was always a funny man. Yeah, I guess so. Always. He, he played the piano and he'd clown around. He still plays nice piano, yeah. Yes, he plays very good Dixie piano. And he always, was always clowning around.
Yeah.
And I knew someday he'd really make it.
Yeah. I guess he's almost ready to retire now. He's not as active I don't think.
No, he doesn't work too much but I don't think he'll retire. Getting older, no, I guess he'll never quit. He gets a big kick out of working.
Yeah, he still comes down here about a year. And he works pretty hard. Yeah. Yeah, he still comes down.
And he's a wonderful fellow.
Yeah, that's what everybody says.
A wonderful, wonderful fellow. No matter the way he sees you, he makes you feel like you his friend.
Yeah.
And I haven't seen him in quite a while. Last time I seen him was here in the Blue Room.
Yeah, just here a couple of years, maybe longer. Yeah. He plays pretty good piano. Did he ever really know much music or just use the piano because he wanted to be an entertainer?
No, no, no, Bill, he was a good piano player. Really? Yes, he studied piano.
Yeah, really intended to be a musician I guess originally then was for a while then. That's right.
Yeah, and they found out that he could do better as a comedian. Yeah. And he became a good comedian.
Yeah, who's the other fellow who plays trombone, I can't think of his name now, in the movies? Jerry Colonna.
Very good musician.

He's another one that's the same type of. Yeah, he was a studio man. Yeah. Yeah. One of this reels about, if you have a few more minutes, it's 12 o'clock, didn't you? No, no, it's all I have about it. I was going to ask a little bit about some of your other travels like the Canada and Europe and the Japan and all that trip if you have a minute. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

So it's good to have this on tape where it'll last forever and hear your voice 50 years from now. I hope they're still interested in this music then. I think they will be. I was going to ask about your trips. There was one trip that they talk about that you went to Canada. That wasn't so long ago, was it? When was it? 1952. About the same time as the Haddock Hall. Right, right after the Haddock Hall. We played a...
